\chapter{El Taller Y La Máquina}
\label{ch:es-maquina}
\hlchaptermodality{434}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that a device has stopped working, what part is missing, where it has gone to be repaired and what I am being charged.}

Read the notice or advert this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el taller]{el taller — where things get mended}

\label{lesson:ES-C434-taller}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el coche}. Say \emph{el trabajo}. The car has stopped working. Name the place it goes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el taller}
\textbf{el taller} — the workshop, the garage in the sense of \emph{repair shop}.

Careful with that English word: \textbf{el garaje} is where you park; \textbf{el taller} is where it gets fixed. English uses \emph{garage} for both and Spanish does not.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el taller} also means a \textbf{workshop} in the other sense — a short practical class. \emph{Un taller de cocina}, \emph{un taller de reparación de bicicletas}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the phrase} & \textbf{what it is} \\
\midrule
llevar el coche al taller & the repair shop \\
un taller de cocina & a hands-on class \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The two meanings share a core that English keeps as well: a place where people work with their hands, rather than sit and listen. If a notice offers you a \emph{taller}, expect to do something, not to watch.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el taller}
  \item I am taking the car to the workshop
  \item the difference between \emph{el taller} and \emph{el garaje}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where the car is repaired? (\textbf{el taller}.) Where it is parked? (\textbf{el garaje}.) What else can a \emph{taller} be? (\textbf{A hands-on class}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la máquina]{la máquina — the word above the others}

\label{lesson:ES-C434-maquina}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la lavadora}. Say \emph{el ordenador}. You can name particular machines. Name the \textbf{kind}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la máquina}
\textbf{la máquina} — the machine.

Stressed on the first syllable, \emph{MÁ-qui-na}, and the written accent marks it.

\begin{cousinweb}
Notice what \textbf{el ordenador} is: \emph{ordenar} plus the doer-ending, the thing that orders. Spanish named the computer after what it \textbf{does}, where English named it after \textbf{counting}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{the computer is} \\
\midrule
Spanish & the orderer \\
English & the counter \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{la máquina} sits above all of these as the general term, and it is the word you need for the ones with no special name: \emph{la máquina de hacer pan}, \emph{la máquina del billete}. When you do not know an appliance's name, \emph{la máquina de} plus what it does will be understood every time.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la máquina}
  \item the washing machine is a machine
  \item the machine for making bread
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The machine? (\textbf{la máquina}.) What does \emph{ordenador} literally name? (\textbf{The one that orders}.) Which syllable is stressed in \emph{máquina}? (\textbf{The first}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la pieza]{la pieza — the part that is missing}

\label{lesson:ES-C434-pieza}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la máquina} and \emph{el taller}. The machine is in the workshop and one small thing is wrong with it. Name that thing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la pieza}
\textbf{la pieza} — the part, the piece, the component.

\emph{Falta una pieza} — a part is missing. \emph{Era una pieza pequeña} — it was a small part. Both are what a repair shop says to you.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la pieza} is wider than English \emph{part}. It also names a \textbf{room} in some regions, and a \textbf{piece of music} almost everywhere.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the phrase} & \textbf{what it means} \\
\midrule
una pieza de la lavadora & a component \\
una pieza de Mozart & a piece of music \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A word that covers several English words is not being vague. It is naming something English happens to split: \emph{a discrete thing that belongs to a larger whole}. Hold that idea and all three uses follow from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la pieza}
  \item a part is missing
  \item it was a small part
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The part? (\textbf{la pieza}.) A part is missing? (\textbf{Falta una pieza}.) What else can a \emph{pieza} be? (\textbf{A piece of music}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la batería]{la batería — the ending that is not one}

\label{lesson:ES-C434-bateria}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la tubería}. You learned that \textbf{-ería} collects. Here is a word that ends the same way. Guess what it collects, then read on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la batería}
\textbf{la batería} — the battery. The one in a car, a phone, a torch.

It also names a \textbf{drum kit}, which is the same idea of \emph{a set of things acting together}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Here the guess fails, and it is worth knowing why.}

There is no Spanish word \emph{bate} that \emph{batería} collects. The word arrived whole from French \textbf{batterie}, where it had been built from \emph{battre}, to beat — a battery of guns, a set of things striking together.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{where the building happened} \\
\midrule
la tubería & in Spanish, from \emph{tubo} \\
la estantería & in Spanish, from \emph{estante} \\
la batería & in French, from \emph{battre} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the resemblance is real but it is \textbf{inherited}, not made here. That is the honest shape of the rule you have been building for three chapters: look for the join, and accept that sometimes the join happened in another language and the pieces never entered this one.

A guess that fails costs you nothing. Not guessing costs you every word you could have read.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la batería}
  \item the car battery
  \item why \emph{tubería} comes apart and \emph{batería} does not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The battery? (\textbf{la batería}.) Is there a Spanish word \emph{bate} under it? (\textbf{No}.) Where was it built? (\textbf{In French}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el cargador]{el cargador — the one that loads}

\label{lesson:ES-C434-cargador}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el móvil}. Say \emph{la batería}. The battery is empty. Name the thing you plug in — and try the ending before you are told.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el cargador}
\textbf{el cargador} — the charger.

\textbf{cargar} — to load, to charge. \textbf{cargar el móvil} is to charge the phone.

\begin{cousinweb}
Fourth time for \textbf{-dor}, and by now it should arrive before the lesson does:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{the doer} \\
\midrule
proveer & el proveedor \\
lavar & la lavadora \\
contar & el contador \\
cargar & el cargador \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{cargar} is worth more than the charger. It means \emph{to load}, and it reaches much further than electricity: \emph{cargar el coche} is to load the car, \emph{la carga} is the load itself, and \emph{no se cobra} from earlier meets it in \emph{hacerse cargo de} — to take charge of something.

The same verb also turns up wherever a shop charges you, which is why \textbf{cobrar} and \textbf{cargar} feel adjacent without being the same word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el cargador}
  \item I have to charge the phone
  \item the battery is empty and I have no charger
  \item all four doer-words you now hold
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The charger? (\textbf{el cargador}.) The verb? (\textbf{cargar}.) What does it mean beyond electricity? (\textbf{To load}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(taller, máquina, pieza, batería …]{(taller, máquina, pieza, batería, cargador) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R434-repaso-maquina}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{the workshop}, \emph{the machine} and \emph{the charger}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the guess, and the one that failed}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{comes apart?} \\
\midrule
\textbf{el cargador} & yes — cargar + \textbf{-dor} \\
\textbf{la batería} & no — built in French, not here \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four chapters have now handed you \textbf{-dor}, \textbf{-ería} and \textbf{-ero}, and \emph{batería} is the first word that wore an ending and did not come apart. Do not read that as a warning against guessing. A guess that fails costs nothing; not guessing costs every word you could have read without help.

\textbf{el taller} and \textbf{el garaje} are the pair to keep straight: English calls both \emph{garage}, Spanish does not. You park in one and your car is repaired in the other.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You could name machines and could not say anything about one that had stopped.} \emph{La lavadora} and \emph{el ordenador} were yours; the place they go, the general word for the kind, the part that is missing, the battery that is flat and the charger you lent somebody were not.

That is most of what a person actually says about a device — and almost none of it is in a beginner's dialogue, because beginners' dialogues are about things that work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all five words
  \item the battery is flat and I have no charger
  \item the car is at the workshop because a part is missing
  \item which of the five did not come apart
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The part? (\textbf{la pieza}.) Where the car is repaired? (\textbf{el taller}.) The charger? (\textbf{el cargador}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(una avería) — the message the shop leaves you}

\label{lesson:ES-C434-sintesis-averia}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la pieza} and \emph{la lavadora}. The message you are about to hear contains both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read it once, as though hearing it on the telephone, then answer.

\begin{quote}
Buenas tardes, llamo del \textbf{taller}. Su \textbf{lavadora} ya está reparada: era una \textbf{pieza} pequeña, así que no le vamos a \textbf{cobrar} la mano de obra. Podemos llevársela el miércoles por la mañana.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what was wrong with it
  \item whether you are being charged for the labour
  \item when they can bring it
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Now the other direction. Say aloud, as if leaving the message yourself:

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the machine does not work and I think a part is missing
  \item I am taking it to the workshop on Monday
  \item I have lent my charger and I need it back
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Four chapters ago none of this was sayable}, and the grammar has not changed once. Every sentence above uses tenses you already had. What was missing was never structure — it was the nouns that ordinary life is actually about.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Who is calling? (\textbf{el taller}.) What was wrong? (\textbf{una pieza pequeña}.) What do you need back? (\textbf{el cargador}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
